t: The accounting principle that requires expenses of a period to be set against the revenues of the same period is known as the:
e: The matching principle pairs expenses with the revenue they help generate in the same period so that profit is correctly measured; it underlies the accrual basis.

t: A firm has total assets of ₹50 lakh and liabilities to outsiders of ₹30 lakh. Using the accounting equation, what is the owners' capital?
e: Assets = Liabilities + Capital, so Capital = 50 minus 30 = ₹20 lakh. This equation reflects the dual aspect concept.

t: A premium receipt of ₹25,000 was completely left out of the books. Which type of error is this?
e: Where a transaction is entirely missed from the books, it is an error of complete omission; the trial balance still agrees because neither debit nor credit was recorded.

t: Which concept guides an accountant to provide for all possible losses but not to anticipate profits?
e: Prudence requires recognising expected losses immediately while recognising gains only when realised, which is why insurers provide for outstanding claims but do not distribute unrealised investment gains.

t: Goods and Services Tax collected from policyholders along with the premium is treated in the insurer's books as:
o: A liability payable to the government, not forming part of premium
e: GST is collected on behalf of the government and is a statutory liability; premium is recognised net of such taxes, so it never enters the Revenue Account as income.

t: Which statement about single premium policies is correct from an accounting perspective?
o: Single premium is spread over the policy term as income
Single premium is treated as a loan from the policyholder
Single premium is credited directly to share capital
Single premium is recognised as income in full when due and the related reserve is created through the valuation
e: The whole single premium is income when due; the long-term liability is captured by the change in valuation of policy liabilities charged in the same Revenue Account.

t: A life insurer spends ₹8 lakh on new office furniture that will be used for several years. How should this outlay be classified?
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Expenditure that creates an asset giving benefit over more than one accounting period is capital expenditure and is shown in the balance sheet, with only depreciation charged to revenue each year.

t: A policy has an annual premium of ₹50,000. The insurer applies a modal loading of 2% for the half-yearly mode. What is the total premium paid in a year under the half-yearly mode?
e: Each half-yearly instalment = 50,000 × 1.02 / 2 = ₹25,500, so the yearly outgo is ₹51,000. The extra ₹1,000 compensates the insurer for delayed receipt and extra collection cost.

t: An interim bonus is paid by a life insurer when:
o: A policy is issued during the year
The insurer records a loss for the year
A participating policy becomes a claim between two valuation dates, for the period since the last bonus declaration
e: Interim bonus covers the gap between the last declared bonus and the date of claim so that policies exiting mid-year are not deprived of their share of surplus.

t: Terminal bonus on a participating policy is normally paid:
o: Every year along with the premium receipt
At the time of policy issue
Only at the time of exit of the policy by maturity or death, as a one-time addition
Only if the policy is surrendered in the first year
e: Terminal (final) bonus is a one-off payment at the time of claim reflecting the policy's share of accumulated surplus, and it is not guaranteed in advance.

t: A loan granted by a life insurer against a policy is normally restricted to:
o: A percentage of the policy's surrender value
The total premiums paid to date
e: Policy loans are secured by the policy and are limited to a proportion (typically up to about 90%) of the surrender value so that the outstanding loan with interest never exceeds the security.

t: A death claim of ₹10,00,000 was settled two months after the prescribed time limit. The bank rate at the beginning of the financial year was 6.5%. What interest is payable to the claimant for the delay?
e: Interest rate = bank rate + 2% = 8.5% p.a.; interest for 2 months = 10,00,000 × 8.5% × 2/12 = ₹14,167 (approximately).

t: After the Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act, 2015, which pair correctly matches the sections of the Insurance Act, 1938 with the business they regulate for expenses of management?
o: Section 40B - general insurance; Section 40C - life insurance
Section 40A - life insurance; Section 40B - general insurance
Section 40B - life insurance; Section 40C - general insurance
Section 41 - life insurance; Section 42 - general insurance
e: Section 40B limits expenses of management in life insurance business and Section 40C does so for general insurance business, with limits specified in IRDAI regulations.

t: Under the IRDAI (Payment of Commission) Regulations, 2023, which statement is correct?
o: Product-wise commission caps continue to be prescribed by IRDAI
Commission is prohibited on renewal premium
Commission cannot exceed 5% of premium on any product
Commission is paid as per a board-approved policy, subject to the overall limit on expenses of management
e: The 2023 regulations removed segment-wise commission caps; insurers frame a board-approved commission policy, but total commission must remain within the overall expenses of management limit.

t: A life insurer's allowable expenses of management for the year work out to ₹1,200 crore while actual expenses were ₹1,260 crore. What amount must be borne by shareholders?
e: The excess of actual over allowable expenses, 1,260 minus 1,200 = ₹60 crore, is charged to the shareholders' Profit and Loss Account rather than to policyholders.

t: Which of the following investments counts towards the minimum 15% requirement for the Life Fund under the IRDAI investment pattern?
e: The pattern requires not less than 15% of the Life Fund in housing and infrastructure investments, reflecting the national priority sectors; overseas investments are not permitted.

t: Income earned on investments held in the policyholders' funds of a life insurer is credited to:
e: Investment income on policyholders' funds belongs to the technical account and is credited to the Revenue Account; only income on shareholders' funds goes to the Profit and Loss Account.

t: A bond with face value ₹100 crore maturing in 4 years is purchased for ₹104 crore to be held to maturity. What amount of premium is amortised each year under the amortised cost method (straight-line)?
o: Nil, premium is written off at purchase
e: The purchase premium of ₹4 crore is amortised over the 4 years remaining to maturity, i.e. ₹1 crore per year, reducing interest income so that the carrying value reaches ₹100 crore at maturity.

t: Which committee is a life insurer required to constitute under the IRDAI investment regulations to oversee its investment policy and operations?
e: The Investment Committee, comprising specified directors, the CEO, CFO, CIO and Appointed Actuary, frames the investment policy and reviews investment performance and compliance.

t: Which section of the Insurance Act, 1938 restricts the expenses of management that a life insurer may incur?
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Section 40B deals with limitation of expenses of management in life insurance business, with the actual limits laid down by IRDAI regulations. Section 40C covers general insurance, Section 41 prohibits rebates and Section 45 relates to repudiation of policies.

t: A life insurer's Pension and General Annuity Fund stands at ₹2,000 crore. What is the minimum amount it must hold in Government securities?
e: The pension and general annuity fund must have at least 20% in Government securities = 0.20 × 2,000 = ₹400 crore, and at least 40% in Government and other approved securities together.

topic: Final Accounts: Revenue Account and Balance Sheet
t: Claims by death, maturity, survival benefits, surrenders and annuities paid by a life insurer are detailed in:
e: Schedule 4 shows benefits paid by type, gross of reinsurance recoveries, with the reinsurance share deducted to arrive at net benefits carried to the Revenue Account.

topic: Final Accounts: Revenue Account and Balance Sheet
t: The pattern of shareholding (promoters Indian and foreign, and others) of a life insurer is disclosed in:
e: Schedule 5 shows share capital and Schedule 5A gives the pattern of shareholding, which is important given the FDI limits applicable to insurers.

topic: Final Accounts: Revenue Account and Balance Sheet
t: Partly paid-up investments, guarantees given and claims not acknowledged as debts by a life insurer are shown as:
o: Contingent liabilities disclosed on the face of the balance sheet
e: Items that may or may not become liabilities depending on future events are disclosed as contingent liabilities in the balance sheet format, not provided for.

topic: Final Accounts: Revenue Account and Balance Sheet
t: In a life insurer's Revenue Account, the item change in valuation of liability in respect of life policies represents:
o: The increase or decrease in mathematical reserves as determined by the Appointed Actuary
e: The movement in policy liabilities between two valuation dates is charged (or credited) to the Revenue Account so that the surplus reflects the true cost of long-term obligations.

topic: Final Accounts: Revenue Account and Balance Sheet
t: A life insurer's Revenue Account shows net premium ₹5,000 crore, investment income ₹1,500 crore, commission ₹300 crore, operating expenses ₹600 crore, benefits paid ₹2,500 crore and change in valuation of policy liabilities ₹2,800 crore. What is the surplus for the year?
The Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2021 raised the permissible foreign direct investment limit in Indian insurance companies to:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). The 2021 amendment raised the FDI cap from 49% (set by the 2015 amendment) to 74% under the automatic route, subject to safeguards on board composition and retention of profits.

t: The master budget of an organisation is:
o: The budget of the largest department
A budget prepared only for capital projects
A consolidated summary of all functional budgets, culminating in a budgeted profit and loss account and balance sheet
e: The master budget integrates sales, expense, capital and cash budgets into projected financial statements and is approved by top management as the overall plan.

t: The main purpose of a cash budget for a life insurer is to:
o: Forecast cash receipts and payments so that surpluses can be invested and shortfalls funded in time
e: The cash budget projects inflows (premiums, investment income, maturities) and outflows (claims, expenses, investments) over short periods to manage liquidity.

t: A branch budgeted operating expenses of ₹8 crore and actual expenses were ₹8.6 crore. Expressed as a percentage of budget, the variance is:
e: Variance = (8.6 minus 8) / 8 = 0.6 / 8 = 7.5%, and since actual expense exceeds budget it is adverse.

t: Human resource accounting attempts to:
o: Record employee salaries as capital expenditure
Measure and report the value of the human capital of an organisation to supplement conventional financial statements
e: Human resource accounting quantifies the investment in and value of employees, which conventional accounts ignore, to aid management and investor decisions.

t: The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) mandated by SEBI for top listed companies in India relates to:
o: Disclosure of environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance
e: BRSR is a sustainability reporting framework covering ESG parameters, part of the move towards non-financial and integrated reporting by Indian corporates, including listed insurers.

topic: Accounting Standard (Applicable to Life Insurance Companies)
t: AS 9 (Revenue Recognition) applies to life insurers in a modified manner because:
o: The IRDAI regulations specifically prescribe when premium income is to be recognised
AS 9 applies only to manufacturing companies
Premium is recognised only on a cash basis
e: The regulations lay down the recognition point for premium (when due, or when units are created) and for reinsurance, so AS 9 operates subject to those specific prescriptions.

topic: Accounting Standard (Applicable to Life Insurance Companies)
t: Which Accounting Standard requires a life insurer to recognise deferred tax assets and liabilities arising from timing differences?
e: AS 22 (Accounting for Taxes on Income) requires recognition of deferred tax on timing differences between accounting income and taxable income, subject to prudence.

topic: Accounting Standard (Applicable to Life Insurance Companies)
t: Costs incurred by a life insurer on acquiring a policy administration software licence with a useful life of five years are treated under:
o: AS 26 - Intangible Assets, capitalised and amortised over useful life
e: Computer software meeting the recognition criteria is an intangible asset under AS 26 and is amortised over its estimated useful life rather than expensed immediately.

t: The lapse ratio of a life insurer measures:
o: The proportion of policies that ceased because premiums were not paid relative to policies in force
e: Lapse ratio is the complement of persistency and indicates the quality of business sold; a high lapse ratio raises acquisition cost recovery concerns.

t: A company has current assets of ₹240 crore and current liabilities of ₹160 crore. Its current ratio is:
e: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities = 240 / 160 = 1.5, indicating short-term liquidity cover.

t: Since 1 April 2021, the standard fire policy for a dwelling in India is:
o: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Bharat Griha Raksha for homes; Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha (up to ₹5 crore) and Bharat Laghu Udyam Suraksha (₹5–50 crore) for enterprises.

t: A persistently high operating expense ratio in a life insurer most directly indicates:
o: That the insurer is spending more to acquire and service each rupee of premium, pressuring profitability and compliance with EoM limits
That claims are being settled faster
That the solvency ratio has risen
e: The expense ratio reflects cost efficiency; a high ratio erodes surplus and may breach the regulatory limit on expenses of management.

t: Assets under management (AUM) of a life insurer broadly represents:
o: The total investments held in policyholders' and shareholders' funds including linked assets
Only the share capital of the insurer
The sum assured of all policies in force
e: AUM is the aggregate of investment assets managed, spanning non-linked policyholders' funds, linked funds and shareholders' funds, and is a key size indicator.

t: The Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act, 2015 raised the foreign investment limit in Indian insurance companies from 26% to:
e: The 2015 amendment raised FDI to 49% (with Indian ownership and control), and the 2021 amendment later raised it to 74%.

t: The Life Insurance Council, which represents life insurers in India, is constituted under:
e: Section 64C of the Insurance Act provides for the Life Insurance Council and the General Insurance Council as bodies of insurers under the Insurance Association of India.

t: Under Section 45 of the Insurance Act 1938, a life insurance policy cannot be called in question on any ground after how many years from the date of issue, revival or rider addition, whichever is later?
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). The 2015 amendment made the three-year bar absolute: after three years no policy may be questioned on any ground, including fraud.

topic: Application of Financial Management Concepts in the Insurance Industry
t: The weighted average cost of capital (WACC) of a company is:
o: The interest rate on its latest borrowing
The average return required by all providers of capital, weighted by the proportion of each source in the capital structure
The dividend yield on its equity shares
The rate of return on government securities
e: WACC blends the cost of equity and after-tax cost of debt by their proportions and serves as the hurdle rate for evaluating projects.

topic: Application of Financial Management Concepts in the Insurance Industry
t: The internal rate of return (IRR) of a project is the discount rate at which:
o: The payback period equals one year
The net present value of the project's cash flows is zero
The cost of capital is minimised
e: IRR equates the present value of inflows with the outlay (NPV = 0); a project is acceptable if its IRR exceeds the cost of capital.

topic: Application of Financial Management Concepts in the Insurance Industry
t: A life insurer expects to receive ₹1,10,000 one year from now. If the appropriate discount rate is 10% per annum, what is the present value of this receipt?
e: Present value = 1,10,000 / (1 + 0.10) = ₹1,00,000. Discounting reverses compounding and is central to actuarial valuation and project appraisal.

t: The maximum deduction available to an individual under Section 80C of the Income-tax Act (including life insurance premium) in a financial year is:
e: Section 80C allows a deduction of up to ₹1,50,000, within the overall ceiling under Section 80CCE which also covers Sections 80CCC and 80CCD(1).

t: With effect from 1 October 2024, tax is deductible at source under Section 194DA on the income component of a taxable life insurance payout at the rate of:
e: The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 reduced the TDS rate under Section 194DA from 5% to 2% on the income component of policy payouts not exempt under Section 10(10D).

topic: Anti-Money Laundering Guidelines and Prevention of Money Laundering (PML) Act
t: Under the IRDAI AML/CFT guidelines, a politically exposed person (PEP) proposing to buy a high-value policy must be subjected to:
o: Enhanced due diligence, including senior management approval for the relationship
No due diligence since PEPs are exempt
Only the standard KYC applicable to all customers
e: PEPs, their family members and close associates are higher-risk customers requiring enhanced due diligence, source-of-funds verification and senior management approval.

topic: Anti-Money Laundering Guidelines and Prevention of Money Laundering (PML) Act
t: The Prevention of Money Laundering Act was enacted in India in the year:
e: The PMLA was enacted in 2002 and brought into force on 1 July 2005; insurers are reporting entities under it and must follow the IRDAI AML/CFT guidelines.
